documents.text:
Expression of concern: Dose-response of iron supplementation on fatigue

The editors have received concerns about the calculation of the dose-response analysis in this article and are investigating.

Retraction and replacement: Dose-response of iron supplementation on fatigue

Following the editors' investigation, this article is retracted and replaced by a corrected version (doi 10.9999/fake.2019.011v2). The dose-response slope in Table 3 was miscalculated: it was reported as 0.45 points per 10 mg and the correct value is 0.28 points per 10 mg. The finding that iron supplementation reduces fatigue is unchanged.

evaluation.change_summary: The paper was first flagged with an expression of concern about its dose-response calculation, then retracted and replaced by a corrected version after the editors' investigation. The error is confined to the main effect size in Table 3 and section 3.3: the slope drops from 0.45 to 0.28 points per 10 mg, and its confidence interval from 0.30 to 0.60 to 0.15 to 0.41. The rest of the paper, including the iron status and adverse event results and the conclusion that fatigue reduction increases with dose, reads the same in the corrected version, and the notice says the finding that iron reduces fatigue is unchanged. This is serious for anyone quoting the size of the effect, who should cite the corrected version, especially as the copy at the original DOI still shows the old number with no retraction mark; the general direction of the finding can still be relied on.
evaluation.evaluation: Your draft cites the paper once, in the Discussion (section 4), where it compares your slope of 0.41 with the paper's 0.45 per 10 mg and treats the closeness as support for your design. That use is directly affected: the paper was retracted and replaced because the 0.45 slope was miscalculated, and the corrected value is 0.28 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.41). The overall impact is low because this is a comparison rather than the basis of your results, and your methods and own estimate do not depend on the paper. The sentence still needs fixing: it should cite the corrected version and give 0.28, and you should reconsider whether your estimate is still "close" and whether that supports your design, since 0.41 now sits at the upper limit of the corrected interval. The direction of the finding is unchanged, so your general statement that fatigue fell more with the higher dose is not in conflict with it.
evaluation.recommendation: Cite the corrected version in your Discussion, change 0.45 to 0.28 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.41), and update reference [7]. Then reconsider whether your 0.41 is still close enough to support your design, since that argument, not just the number, is affected.

alerts.what_changed: The editors published an expression of concern saying they had received concerns about how the paper's dose-response analysis was calculated and were investigating. It reported no outcome at that point.

affected_parts.part: Dose-response analysis of fatigue (Table 3, Results section 3.3)
affected_parts.findings_affected: The estimated reduction in fatigue score per 10 mg of daily oral iron, reported as 0.45 points per 10 mg (95% CI 0.30 to 0.60), and claims about how large the dose-response effect is.

alerts.reason: An expression of concern about the calculation of the main analysis puts that result in doubt while the investigation runs. The later retraction notice in this report closes the investigation by confirming the error.

The corrected version also changes the confidence interval from 0.30 to 0.60 to 0.15 to 0.41; no other content difference from the stored paper was found apart from its title label and a replacement banner.

affected_parts.part: Table 3 and Results section 3.3: dose-response slope of the Fatigue Severity Index
affected_parts.findings_affected: Any statement citing the size of the effect of iron dose on fatigue: 0.45 points per 10 mg (95% CI 0.30 to 0.60) is wrong; the corrected value is 0.28 points per 10 mg (95% CI 0.15 to 0.41). The direction is unchanged: fatigue reduction still increases with dose between 20 and 60 mg.

alerts.reason: This is a retraction and replacement where a corrected version exists: the primary effect size falls by about a third, but the notice says the finding that iron reduces fatigue stands, and the corrected paper's conclusions are unchanged. Citations should move to the corrected version, because the copy at the original DOI downloaded on 2026-10-02 still shows 0.45 with no retraction mark.
